lead: Unit testing checks one module alone, using a driver to call it and stubs to replace the modules it calls. Integration testing checks whether modules work together, using a chosen order and interface tests. Both exist because defects hide at two places: inside a module and at the boundary between modules. A unit test gives a fast, repeatable pass or fail for one small piece of code. Integration testing then finds wrong parameter order, missing data, incompatible types and timing faults that a unit test cannot see. The same harness ideas appear in everyday work: a payment module is tested with a fake bank, then joined to the real billing flow.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for test cases and defects, Chapter 4.4 for black-box test design, and Unit 3 coupling for interfaces.

sections.h3: Unit testing and the test harness

blocks.text: Unit testing checks one module, class or function on its own. The unit is the smallest part that can be compiled and called. A defect found inside one small module is cheap to locate; a defect that escapes into the full product is costly.

Unit test planning lists the units to test, each unit's inputs and outputs, the test data, and the expected result. Designing unit tests uses the detailed design of the module: its interface, data structures and logic. Black-box tests come from the specification; white-box tests come from the code, as Chapter 4.3 and Chapter 4.4 explain. A unit test case has an input, a precondition, the call, and the expected output.

A test harness is the software that runs a unit test. A driver is a small program that calls the unit under test, passes inputs and records the result. A stub is a fake module that the unit calls; it returns fixed, simple values. Some syllabi call the harness a unit test harness. The driver replaces the caller; the stub replaces a called module. Do not swap them: the driver calls the unit, the stub is called by the unit.

The harness runs the tests, compares actual with expected, and records pass or fail. A failure is logged with the input, expected value, actual value and a defect report. A unit test should not use a real database, network or payment gateway. Such a test is slow, hard to repeat, and it tests more than one unit. Replace those external parts with stubs.

Integration testing checks whether modules work together. A unit can pass alone and still fail when it calls another module with a different parameter order, a missing field or a different data type. Integration testing finds these interface defects and checks that the assembled build matches the design.
Big-bang integration puts all modules together and tests the whole. It is quick to start and hard to debug: when one test fails, many modules could be the cause. It suits very small systems only.

Top-down integration starts with the top control module. Modules below it are replaced by stubs. Test the top, replace one stub with the real module, then the next. It needs stubs, not drivers. It finds control and interface problems early. A low-level module may be tested late.

Bottom-up integration starts with the lowest modules. Each low-level module is called by a driver that supplies inputs. Test the bottom, combine with the next level, and use a driver until the top exists. It needs drivers, not stubs. It finds low-level defects early, but the top control logic is tested late.

Sandwich or hybrid integration combines top-down and bottom-up. The top is tested downward with stubs; the bottom is tested upward with drivers; the two meet in a middle layer. It balances early testing of control and low-level code.

Incremental builds add one module or a small group at a time and rerun the integration tests after each build. This shows which build introduced a failure. Integration test planning chooses the order, the interfaces to test, the stubs and drivers needed, and the data for each interface. Record pass or fail for each interface test, not just for the whole build.

sections.h3: Interface defects and integration test planning

blocks.text: Integration tests focus on interfaces. Common interface defects are: wrong parameter order, where calculateGST(rate, amount) is called with the arguments reversed; missing data, where a field is absent or null; incompatible types, where a string "18" is passed where an integer 18 is expected; and timing, where one module expects data before another module produces it. A wrong parameter order can produce a plausible but wrong answer, so interface tests need boundary values and exact expected outputs.

Designing integration tests follows the chosen order. For each pair of modules, list the values passed, the values returned, and the error cases. For top-down order, write stubs with fixed returns. For bottom-up order, write drivers that call the lower module. For sandwich order, prepare both. The test data should include normal values, boundary values and invalid values.

Integration test planning names the modules, the build order, the interfaces in each build, the stubs and drivers, the test environment, and the pass/fail record. Keep the unit tests and rerun them after integration repairs; that is regression testing, covered in Chapter 4.7. Unit testing answers 'does this module work alone?' Integration testing answers 'do these modules work together?' System testing, which checks the whole product against requirements, comes in Chapter 4.6.

spec.title: Unit under test with a driver
spec.aria: Block diagram: a test driver calls calculateGST and also sends the result to a result log.

examples.question: A module calculateGST(amount, rate) returns amount × rate ÷ 100. Billing calls calculateGST and Invoice. (a) Design a unit test for calculateGST with amount = ₹1,000 and rate = 18. State the driver call and expected result. (b) In top-down integration, Billing is tested first with a stub Invoice returning ₹1,180. Billing computes total = invoice amount + GST on that amount at 18%. Find the GST and total. (c) Name one driver and one stub here, and say what unit versus integration testing checks.
steps: Unit inputs: amount = ₹1,000, rate = 18. Expected GST = 1,000 × 18 ÷ 100 = ₹180.
Driver call: calculateGST(1000, 18). Compare actual with ₹180; pass if equal, else log the defect.
Integration: Billing is the unit under test. The Invoice stub returns ₹1,180. Billing calls calculateGST(1180, 18). GST = 1,180 × 18 ÷ 100 = ₹212.40.

Driver: the integration test driver that calls Billing. Stub: Invoice returning ₹1,180. Unit testing checks calculateGST alone; integration testing checks Billing's calls to calculateGST and Invoice, including argument order and return values.
examples.answer: Unit expected GST is ₹180; integration GST is ₹212.40 and total is ₹1,392.40. The driver calls the unit; a stub is called by the unit under test (here Billing calls the Invoice stub). Unit testing checks calculateGST alone; integration testing checks Billing with Invoice.
examples.check:
amount = 1000
rate = 18
unit_gst = amount * rate / 100
print(unit_gst)
invoice = 1180
integration_gst = invoice * rate / 100
print(integration_gst)
total = invoice + integration_gst
print(total)

traps: Swapping driver and stub: a driver calls the unit under test; a stub is called by the unit under test.
Using a real database, network or payment gateway inside a unit test; replace it with a stub so the test is fast and isolated.
Treating top-down integration as needing drivers: top-down needs stubs; bottom-up needs drivers.
Assuming a module that passes its unit test will pass integration; interface defects appear only when modules are joined.
Testing only normal values at interfaces; wrong parameter order and incompatible types often show up on boundary or invalid values.

quiz.a: A program that calls the unit under test, supplies inputs and records the result.
Whether modules work together and exchange data correctly across interfaces.

quiz.q: Why does top-down integration need stubs?
quiz.a: Lower modules are not ready, so stubs stand in and return fixed values while the top is tested.

quiz.q: calculateGST(amount, rate) = amount × rate ÷ 100. Find the expected result for amount = ₹2,500, rate = 12.
Billing total = invoice + GST at 18%. The Invoice stub returns ₹2,000. Find GST and total.
A unit passes alone but fails in integration. Give two likely causes and one test to locate the fault.
quiz.a: Wrong parameter order or incompatible type at the interface. Add an interface test that logs each argument and return and compares with the expected value.

quiz.q: A layered system has stable database modules and a new user interface on top. Which integration order is better, and why?
quiz.a: Sandwich or hybrid: test the stable bottom upward with drivers and the new top downward with stubs, then join in the middle. This tests both ends early.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, unit tests are often written with frameworks such as JUnit, pytest or NUnit and run on every commit in a continuous integration pipeline. Teams use test doubles such as mocks, fakes and stubs, and contract tests to check interfaces between services. Mutation testing measures whether unit tests catch small injected faults. Search for 'test doubles', 'contract testing' and 'mutation testing' to go further.
